title: Meet ProPublica’s 2026 Class of Emerging Reporters
author: Talia Buford
content:
ProPublica’s Emerging Reporters Program provides support and mentorships to
college students who are pursuing careers in investigative journalism and need
additional training and financial support to help advance their goals.

Participants receive a $9,000 stipend, a trip to the annual NICAR
investigative journalism conference, occasional training and presentations by
speakers. They’ll also be paired one-on-one with ProPublica journalists who
can help counsel them on stories, build their connections in the industry and
expose them to the varied paths that careers in investigative journalism can
take. Past Emerging Reporters have gone on to work at The New York Times, The
Associated Press, Fresnoland, Capital B, The Tributary and other outlets.

Our goal is to encourage the next generation of journalists who seek to shine
a light on abuses of power and produce stories with moral force that provoke
change. In choosing the class, we look for students who demonstrate an early
dedication to journalism as a career, through internships, work at local news
outlets or work at campus publications. And where those opportunities — which
are often unpaid — aren’t accessible, we look for other ways the student has
shown an eagerness and a drive to learn the craft.

This year’s class of exceptional student journalists are from schools in
Illinois, Texas, Nebraska, Iowa and New York.

Meet our 2026 class:

### Annisyn Krebs-Carr (she/her)

![A woman with long blonde braids smiles at the camera and wears a black top
and a necklace with a silver pendant.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Annisyn-Krebs-Carr-resized.jpg?w=752)Courtesy of
Annisyn Krebs-Carr

Annisyn Krebs-Carr is a senior at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign
studying journalism and animal sciences. She is a reporter for Illinois Public
Media Student Newsroom, where she reports on the ongoing housing crisis in
Champaign-Urbana. Previously, she served as the arts and entertainment editor
at The Daily Illini, the independent newspaper at the university. She is now
the managing editor and oversees content produced by the entire newsroom. In
2026, she interned for St. Louis Public Radio and formed relationships with
the investigative reporters at NPR’s Midwest Newsroom. This is where she
developed a deeper appreciation for investigative journalism. As she continues
her journalism career, she wants to focus on how the criminal justice system
has failed, and continues to fail, Black people. She also wants to explore how
environmental racism has impacted lower-income communities. After graduation,
she hopes to work in a public media newsroom and report on local stories while
honing her investigative journalism skills. Long term, Annisyn hopes to build
a dedicated career as an investigative journalist in public media.

### Jessica Meza (she/her)

![A woman with shoulder-length wavy dark brown hair smiles at the camera. She
wears glasses, a green tank top and a silver
necklace.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jessica-Meza-
resized.jpg?w=752)Courtesy of Jessica Meza

Jessica Meza is a senior at the University of Nebraska, Lincoln studying
journalism, advertising and public relations. Jessica works across mediums,
including in data visualizations, video, print and social media, with an
emphasis on audio reporting. Jessica hopes to begin her career in
investigative, in-depth reporting, focusing on marginalized communities. She
hopes to use her reporting to amplify the voice of people facing hidden
injustices in her community. Other interests include housing, immigration and
food reporting. Jessica currently works at Nebraska Public Media as a
reporting intern. She previously interned at NPR’s Midwest Newsroom and, as
the Hortencia Zavala Foundation intern, wrote for The Fulcrum and the Latino
News Network. In 2025, she was part of the team at Nebraska News Service that
was awarded a regional Society of Professional Journalists Mark of Excellence
Award for its investigative project on missing and murdered marginalized
women.

### Lajward Zahra (she/her)

![A woman with long black hair wears a green top and smiles at the camera. Her
face is dramatically lit and she is in front of a building and out-of-focus
trees.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Lajward-Zahra-
resized.jpg?w=752)Courtesy of Lajward Zahra

Lajward Zahra is a senior English major at Rice University in Houston,
originally from El Paso, Texas. Her reporting focuses on politics, immigration
and the environment, particularly in Texas. She is a 2025 writing fellow at
The Nation and has written for the magazine since 2023. She previously
interned with the Houston Chronicle editorial board in summer 2025, reporting
and writing on local and state politics, including the Texas Republican Party
convention, among other issues. Lajward’s freelance work has also appeared in
publications including The American Prospect, Teen Vogue, Business Insider,
Rewire News Group and Scalawag. She was a 2024 Asian American Journalists
Association Voices fellow.

### Thai Theodoro (she/her)

![A woman with shoulder-length blonde hair smiles at the camera. She wears
glasses and a red patterned blouse and is in front of out-of-focus
buildings.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Thaina-
Theodoro-resized.jpg?w=752)Courtesy of Thai Theodoro

Originally from Brazil, Thai Theodoro studies political science with a
concentration in Latin American studies at Grinnell College in Iowa. Now in
her senior year, she is the managing editor of The Scarlet & Black, Grinnell’s
independent student newspaper. Thai has interned at The Boston Globe, the Des
Moines Register and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, and her reporting has been
published in dozens of newspapers across the country. She is a member of the
New York Times Corps and a former participant in the National Association of
Hispanic Journalists’ Student Project. Thai is passionate about telling untold
stories, pursuing investigative reporting with the power to challenge the
status quo, using the three languages she speaks to reach underrepresented
communities, and, of course, writing the occasional quirky story.

### Tsehai Alfred (she/her)

![A woman with long, dark, curly hair wears a black long-sleeved shirt and
smiles at the camera. She is standing in front of a white pillar, and a stone-
and-brick building can be seen in the
background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Tsehai-
Alfred-resize.jpg?w=752)Courtesy of Tsehai Alfred

Tsehai Alfred is a senior at Columbia University studying English. She is the
150th editor-in-chief and president of the Columbia Daily Spectator, the
campus newspaper, and is also an intern on CNN’s criminal justice team. Over
the summer, she was a Dow Jones News Fund intern at VTDigger, an
accountability-focused newsroom in Vermont, investigating the troubled
integration of AI into healthcare, a struggling dairy farming industry, and
soaring police use-of-force payouts. Previously, she has interned at City &
State New York, covering the 2025 mayoral race and city council; at PBS News
as a Gwen Ifill Journalism Fellow; and at her local news outlet, the Virgin
Islands Consortium. Her reporting interests include local government, economic
inequality, and political and corporate accountability.
